summary: Deep technical discussion focused on architecture-specific tuning for Llama, Mistral, and Qwen families; MoE routing costs and tradeoffs; RoPE scaling and numeric/quantization interactions; deployment considerations for VPC/on-prem and KV cache/sharding. topics: Model-specific kernel choices (Llama vs Mistral vs Qwen)
transcript:
[00:00] Alex Kim: Okay, good afternoon everyone, thanks for carving out the time. Today's a deep dive, we wanted to focus on model-architecture specific tuning — Llama, Mistral, Qwen — and then the tricky bits like MoE routing overhead and RoPE scaling. Samir is going to lead the benchmarks discussion.

[00:18] Samir Patel: Hey all, hi Priya, Marcus. Quick note I'm going to jump between high level and microbench. Feel free to interrupt.

[00:29] Priya Nair: Thanks, we mostly want to understand the perf tradeoffs — cost vs latency — and what we'd need to run for an on-prem pilot.

[00:36] Samir Patel: Totally. Start with MoE: for Qwen-MoE style models the gating has two main costs — compute for the gate forward/backward and the memory & communication for routing activations to experts. At inference-only workloads the backward is gone but the forwarding routing still adds overhead: scatter/gather and extra all-to-all when experts live on different GPUs.

[01:05] Marcus Chen: So is the routing cost basically linear in number of tokens, or is there a fixed hit at each request?

[01:12] Samir Patel: Good question. It's both — there is a fixed per-request scheduling/dispatch cost (latency overhead like tens of microseconds depending on infra), plus token-level costs for the actual routing. For small batch or low tokens-per-request, the fixed dispatch dominates. For high throughput with batching, the per-token costs amortize. We've seen in our internal tests a 10-30% tail-latency delta for single-GPU MoE vs dense baseline for similar top-1 quality, but that varies with expert placement and network topology.

[01:45] Elena Gomez: We plan a latency SLO of 200ms p95 for chat workloads, and peak QPS around 120 QPS. Is MoE a non-starter for that?

[01:55] Samir Patel: Not necessarily. If you co-locate the experts (expert sharding) and avoid cross-node all-to-all by fitting the model on a single multi-GPU node with NVLink, the routing cost can be kept low. The trade is you need bigger nodes (8x A100 / H100) or model parallel chunking. But if you're on multi-node with RDMA but not NVLink, we do see more unpredictable tails because of networking.

[02:20] Alex Kim: And don't forget batching behavior — Redwood's continuous batching and request coalescing can help amortize gating costs. We also support policy-based routing: if latency-sensitive requests come in, we can route them to a dense variant instead of MoE to keep p99 bounded.

[02:39] Priya Nair: What about expert count? Is fewer experts always better for latency?

[02:44] Samir Patel: Fewer experts reduces the scatter/gather footprint but can harm quality. There's a sweet spot: for a 30B MoE model we've seen quality plateauing past ~32 experts in our eval sets; however, cost per token rises with experts because of routing table sizes and memory traffic. We'll share the microbenchmarks.

[03:03] Dana Ruiz: Quick aside on KV cache — we've seen some customers misinterpret prefix caching behavior. If you shard KV across devices you need either a cross-device aggregation or you pin a request to the device that has the prefix. Both approaches have tradeoffs for memory and latency.

[03:22] Elena Gomez: We've been seeing KV cache blow up memory for long-context summaries; any quick wins?

[03:28] Samir Patel: A few: rolling prefix eviction (keep the most recent N tokens), compressed KV with fp16 for keys/values, or hybrid caching where we keep keys in-memory and values compressed to reduce footprint. For long contexts, we also recommend selective prefix caching — only cache spans that are likely to be reused.

[03:51] Marcus Chen: On RoPE scaling — last time we tested Llama-2 70B we hit degradation at longer sequences. What's Redwood's guidance?

[03:59] Alex Kim: Right, RoPE/rotary embeddings can underflow/over-rotate with longer sequences if the model wasn't trained with longer RoPE positions. For models like Llama family you often see drifting attention patterns when extrapolating beyond training length. Our approach: 1) use RoPE scaling techniques (linear/exponential decay adjustments), 2) evaluate numeric effects with quantization — q4/q8 can exacerbate phase errors, and 3) when possible, prefer models with explicit long-context training, or apply prefix-summarization strategies.

[04:28] Samir Patel: Adding to that — for Qwen we observed more robust RoPE extrapolation in their newer families, but Mistral's sparse attention in some sizes interacts oddly; the kernel selection matters. With certain kernels the rotary math gets reordered and rounding creates subtle drift. So kernel selection + quantization config matter together.

[04:52] Priya Nair: Can you give an example where quantization made RoPE worse?

[04:56] Samir Patel: Yeah — in a q4_0-style config we saw phase errors increase after 2048 tokens, p95 attention score drop by ~4-6% relative to fp16 baseline for a specific Llama model. Switching to q8 or nf4 improved it. So the recommendation is: if you rely on long RoPE contexts, validate end-to-end with quantized weights and the same tokenizer/pipeline as prod. We'll share the reproducible tests.

[05:24] Marcus Chen: What about kernel choice? You mentioned that earlier.

[05:27] Samir Patel: Kernels: some vendors use fused rotary ops, others break it out. Fused ops can reduce rounding if implemented carefully, but on certain backends the fused kernel does extra temporaries that increase memory pressure. For Mistral, the attention block shape and preferred GEMM layout differs — we pick kernels dynamically based on sequence length distribution and hardware. That's the compilation step in our runtime.

[05:53] Elena Gomez: For quantization — are your recommendations general (int8) or model-specific?

[05:58] Alex Kim: Mix — model specific. Llama family typically tolerates int8 and nf4 quite well; Mistral sometimes needs slightly higher precision on feedforward dense layers (q8) to avoid quality regressions. Qwen also has its quirks around layernorm ordering and needs a careful per-layer qconfig. We provide per-model recommended qconfigs in our model catalog, but always advise benchmark runs with your prompt sets.

[06:25] Priya Nair: For an on-prem pilot, what infra should we provision? We plan to run on an internal cluster with 4xH100 per node and Mellanox HDR interconnect.

[06:36] Samir Patel: 4x H100 with NVLink inside the node is a good starting point for dense 70B and some MoE variants if you partition experts. But for large MoE that needs many experts, you'll want 8x GPUs per node or a smaller dense fallback. Mellanox HDR is fine but you have to watch for all-to-all patterns. If you can map experts to GPUs to avoid inter-node comms, it's best. Also ensure your RDMA setup has low jitter; we saw perf cliffs with misconfigured MTU or flow-control.

[07:05] Marcus Chen: Any gotchas for VPC deployment vs fully on-prem?

[07:09] Alex Kim: On VPC hosted variants, Redwood handles the control plane and we integrate with your KMS for keys. On private/on-prem you run the control plane in a VPC or air-gapped setup; the main gotchas are: 1) KMS/HSM integration (you need a reachable endpoint or proxy), 2) audit/log shipping to your SIEM — we support local log sinks but set expectations on bandwidth, and 3) network topology for model parallel comms.

[07:38] Priya Nair: Security questions — SOC2 and SAML.

[07:41] Alex Kim: We'll send SOC 2 Type II and our SAML docs in the follow-up. For on-prem we can enable SSO to your IdP and RBAC matrix. We'll include recommended audit filters so you don't overshoot retention costs.

[07:57] Elena Gomez: Back to batching — how does Redwood's continuous batching affect latency? We want low tail but good throughput.

[08:05] Dana Ruiz: I can take that — continuous batching basically collects requests up to a latency budget and coalesces kernels. For short budgets (<20ms) you can still get good throughput with minimal added latency. For p99 optimization you can profile request length distributions and set separate buckets per model/route. We also support per-route latency caps that will short-circuit batching and send to a low-latency pool.

[08:34] Priya Nair: How do you handle multitenant KV cache memory isolation?

[08:38] Samir Patel: We isolate KV caches per-tenant and evict based on tenant quotas; we can also pin hot prefixes to faster storage or DRAM tiers. For on-prem, you control the physical memory layout but Redwood's runtime exposes knobs for eviction policy and per-route cache size.

[08:56] Marcus Chen: ROI question — do you typically see cost savings from quantization + batching that offset MoE complexity?

[09:03] Alex Kim: Generally yes. For many conversational workloads, q4/q8 plus aggressive batching and prefix caching reduces per-token cost by 40-60% vs fp16 naive runs. MoE can give step-changes in compute efficiency for quality if you can accept the deployment complexity. For some customers the combination (dense + quant + cache) is enough; for others, the MoE quality-per-cost is worth the extra infra work.

[09:28] Elena Gomez: Any specific benchmark we should run to compare Llama vs Mistral vs Qwen for our prompts?

[09:34] Samir Patel: We recommend: 1) the end-to-end latency with your 50-100 representative prompts (measure cold/warm with KV cache), 2) throughput with variable batch sizes to identify the knee, 3) quantized vs fp16 quality eval (ROUGE/BLEU/ROPT where relevant) and 4) stress test MoE routing with synthetic high-concurrency to observe tail behavior. We'll provide a script to run these.

[10:00] Priya Nair: Great. On RoPE — you mentioned scaling techniques — can you sketch them quickly?

[10:06] Samir Patel: Sure: common approaches — linear RoPE scaling where you scale the positions by a factor; sinusoidal interpolation; or using rotary decay where the rotation speed is reduced for higher positions. There's also position interpolation strategies. Implementation-sensitive bits: do it in fp32 before quant rounding, and make sure fused kernels preserve the math ordering.

[10:34] Marcus Chen: For our pilot we'd prefer to keep models mostly stock. Any quick wins to avoid retraining?

[10:39] Alex Kim: Yes: 1) use prefix summary for ultra-long contexts, 2) pick slightly larger model with quantization (better quality/latency trade), 3) use a dense fallback for the lowest-latency route and MoE for throughput-oriented routes, and 4) tune batch budgets. These reduce the need for any model fine-tuning.

[11:02] Elena Gomez: Can you also explain the memory layout for experts — do you replicate some parameters?

[11:07] Samir Patel: We typically shard experts (each GPU holds a subset) and replicate the gating & router metadata. The FFN weights for experts are large; you don't replicate them across devices, otherwise memory explodes. There are hybrid strategies where you partially replicate small hot experts to avoid cross-device comms, but that's only for very hot-hot experts.

[11:30] Priya Nair: Is there an easy way to fallback from MoE to dense automatically?

[11:34] Alex Kim: Redwood supports policy-based automatic fallback. You can define latency SLOs and the runtime will route to a pre-defined dense variant if the MoE cluster's tail latency rises. It's a standard canary/fallback pattern in our rollout config.

[11:52] Marcus Chen: Do you support mixed-precision KV (keys in fp16 values in int8) safely?

[11:58] Samir Patel: Yes but be careful — mixing types can introduce small accuracy perturbations in attention scores. Keys in fp16 and values in int8 compressed generally works for generation tasks; for retrieval or dense matching tasks you'd prefer fp16/32 keys. Always validate with your evals.

[12:18] Priya Nair: For the MoE microbenchmarks you mentioned — what configs should we expect in the artifact?

[12:23] Samir Patel: We'll include: model size, expert count, gating top-k (1 vs 2), per-expert capacity, batch size sweep, sequence lengths (128/512/1024/2048), placement (co-located experts vs distributed), and network topology notes. We'll attach raw logs and a summary CSV.

[12:48] Elena Gomez: Any hint on expected numbers — even ballpark — for routing overhead at 512 tokens?

[12:54] Samir Patel: Ballpark: on a co-located 8x H100 node we saw routing overhead of ~8-15% extra time at 512 tokens compared to dense baseline for similar effective quality; on multi-node that can rise to 20-45% depending on all-to-all. Numbers vary a lot with expert count and batching, so treat as indicative.

[13:18] Alex Kim: We'll try to make the benchmark reproducible. We'll also include the exact kernel build flags and the runtime config so you can replicate on-prem.

[13:27] Marcus Chen: Regarding RoPE and quantization — do you recommend testing q4 first or q8?

[13:32] Samir Patel: Start with q8 for long-context-sensitive models, q4 for short- to medium-context. If you see quality drop with q4, try nf4 or a per-layer q8 on sensitive layers (usually the first FFN and the attention query/key/value projections).

[13:53] Priya Nair: Is there automation for per-layer qconfig selection?

[13:57] Dana Ruiz: We have an automated quant sweep that profiles per-layer sensitivity using a small calibration set; it suggests a recommended qconfig. It's not perfect but it accelerates the process. We'll share the tool and the config we used for the microbenchmarks.

[14:15] Elena Gomez: Network tuning — you mentioned MTU. Any other low-level settings we should watch?

[14:20] Samir Patel: Make sure flow control is enabled, check for bufferbloat on switches, and tune NIC ring sizes for RDMA. For NVLink topologies, check peer-to-peer mappings. Also ensure your PCIe firmware is up to date; we've seen perf cliffs due to firmware bugs.

[14:42] Marcus Chen: For the on-prem pilot, would Redwood run the benchmarks or do we run them and hand you the logs?

[14:49] Alex Kim: We can do either. For initial speed, we can run the Redwood-managed benchmark on your infra (with an ephemeral agent) or provide the scripts for you to run and upload artifacts. For security-sensitive setups you might prefer running locally and sharing logs.

[15:05] Priya Nair: Let's have you run the first pass since you're already tuned in, then we'll replicate.

[15:09] Alex Kim: Sounds good. We'll need access details to the node(s) and a service account for the benchmark runner. We'll send a checklist.

[15:16] Elena Gomez: In terms of cost, what's rough delta between dense q4 and MoE for same quality?

[15:22] Samir Patel: Varies a lot. For certain tasks MoE can be 2-3x cheaper per token for similar quality if you can pack experts efficiently (because compute per-token is lower if only a few experts activate). But when you account for infra idleness and routing overhead it compresses — sometimes end-to-end it's 1.2-1.8x cheaper. We'll show cost-model spreadsheets.

[15:45] Marcus Chen: Any final tips on RoPE scaling?

[15:48] Samir Patel: Always measure using the same tokenization, do fp32 baseline runs, test per-layer quant sensitivity, and if you need to extrapolate RoPE beyond training length, prefer interpolation/decay approaches that were shown to be stable. And bake the fallback policy into the runtime so you can route long-session requests to models trained for longer contexts.

[16:10] Alex Kim: Okay, recap — action items and next steps: Samir will run microbenchmarks and share results, Alex will send RoPE and quant notes + SOC2/SAML, Priya to share SLOs and infra details, schedule pilot planning next week. Anything else?

[16:25] Priya Nair: That covers it, thanks.

[16:28] Elena Gomez: Thanks everyone.

[16:30] Alex Kim: We'll follow up with artifacts. Bye.

[16:33] -- End of recording --

Notes: transcription has minor errors in product names (e.g., "rope" vs RoPE, "KV cash" occasional mis-typing). We intentionally kept verbatim fragments to preserve meeting artifact realism.
